original_value: In this work, we propose an entirely learning-based method to automatically synthesize text sequence in natural images leveraging conditional adversarial networks. As vanilla GANs are clumsy to capture structural text patterns, directly employing GANs for text image synthesis typically results in illegible images. Therefore, we design a two-stage architecture to generate repeated characters in images. Firstly, a character generator attempts to synthesize local character appearance independently, so that the legible characters in sequence can be obtained. To achieve style consistency of characters, we propose a novel style loss based on variance-minimization. Secondly, we design a pixel-manipulation word generator constrained by self-regularization, which learns to convert local characters to plausible word image. Experiments on SVHN dataset and ICDAR, IIIT5K datasets demonstrate our method is able to synthesize visually appealing text images. Besides, we also show the high-quality images synthesized by our method can be used to boost the performance of a scene text recognition algorithm.

result.paraphrase: We present a fully learning-based approach for automatically synthesizing text sequences in natural images using conditional adversarial networks. Because vanilla GANs struggle to model structural text patterns, direct GAN-based text image synthesis usually produces illegible results. To address this, we introduce a two-stage architecture for generating repeated characters in images. First, a character generator independently synthesizes local character appearances so that legible character sequences can be formed. To maintain stylistic consistency across characters, we propose a new style loss based on variance minimization. Second, a pixel-manipulation word generator, constrained by self-regularization, learns to transform local characters into plausible word images. Experiments on the SVHN, ICDAR, and IIIT5K datasets show that our method can synthesize visually appealing text images. We also demonstrate that the high-quality images produced by our method can improve the performance of a scene text recognition algorithm.
